The house is built
along lines of the most orthodox of the orthodox gay nineties atrocities.
Its architecture, if
it deserves even the mention of architecture, 1s
an amazing conglomeration of square, rounded and triangular shaped

Page 2.
appendages, do-funnies and gelapies.
The windows are colonial in
type ana the giass various
shades of red and blue - like the
windows af the deacons building committee puts in a new church
until some rich parishoner can be high jacked into putting out
for a stained glass job.
Inside the woodwork was all heavily
carved in Chinese designs which clash violently with the Grand
Rapids golden oak furniture.
The rickety chandeliers reminiscent of
days swayed as we walked over the dusty floors from one
deserted room to another.
Outside the garden was entirely different.
A moon door let us
through a high wall and there within the confines of that old
moss covered wall enclosing an acre or more of ground was a garden
such as described by Lin Yu Tang in his "My Country and my People"
A small pond - walks - flowers - little temples and many benches
in quiet spots.
The garden is better maintained than the deserted
house because the simewhat impoverished relations who remain at
the old village love this spot to which they retire from their
nearby Chinese houses for peace and seclusion.
Ki Chun took me
to the Chinese house where his father moved from Shanghai when
Ki Was five years old.
It seems a soothsayer gave Ki's father
some advice which led
to the making of a fortune in his early
twenties but the soothsayer also told him that he would die at
age 30.
Therefore in his 29th year he made his brother trustee
of his fortune and repaired to his old home prepared to die.
However he lived through the 30th year and then returned to
Shanghai to resume business activities with his brother but from
that day to this the brother's fortunes have remained merged and
no distribution has ever been made. Ki's uncle is still living.
When he dies the combined fortune will be divided between the two
families with Ki receiving half as the head of and for the account
of his family - meaning his brothers and sisters.
Ki was expected
on his visit to make a present to all his poor relatives and accord-
ingly we smuggled some silver from Macao because Ki
said those poor
people still look upon paper money as "stage money".
the money to his old nurse - several hundred dollars - receiving
no receipt, issuing no instructions and demanding no accounting•
Ki said very simply - "She is loyal to me and I shall always take
care of her - she knows just how much to give each relative and
they will all be happy."
Then he added laughingly - "Tomorrow
we come to worship,
all my relatives will be glad to see me
and I will be a big shot."
We visited the room where Ki got his first schooling,
examined the armory
where his father's seven old rifles still stand
ready to repel a bandit attack,
and got out a lot of old family
pictures in which Ki's grandfather's twenty-three concubines were
naturally very much in evidence.
a real
glimpse behind the scenes of the old time
Chinese
family life and I thoroughly enjoyed the afternoon.
We are now approaching Shanghai and I will have to go to
work.
